title: Operating model: who decides, who does the work and who checks it?
short: Name one accountable person for each of six core security processes and fit the whole operating model on two pages.
answer: This quarter, write down on two pages who decides, who does the work and who checks it for six core processes, from patching to exceptions, and have management approve it. Buy the work wherever that is cheaper, but keep decisions, risk acceptance and supplier oversight with your own named people.
audience: Heads of security and CISOs, IT leads who own security, and the managing directors they report to

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Give each core process one accountable name.
items.text: Name one A and the people who do the work for each of the six processes below. NIST suggests documenting who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed[^csfie].

items.title: Write down who decides what.
items.text: The BSI asks management to settle which cyber decisions need its approval[^bsicurr]. Add who may accept which risk, grant which exception and isolate which system.

items.title: Separate doing from checking.
items.text: Assurance isn't credible if the reviewer designs or operates the process, the IIA says[^iia3l]. Don't let the people who run systems audit them or approve their own exceptions.

items.title: Buy the work, keep the decisions.
items.text: Entities that outsource all their IT stay responsible, and contracts alone aren't enough, the BSI says[^bsifaq]. Keep risk acceptance and supplier oversight with named staff.

items.title: Fit it on two pages and get it approved.
items.text: Regulation 2024/2690 has management review roles at planned intervals and after significant incidents or changes[^ir2690]. Review yours yearly and after every reorganization.

blocks.title: Write it down in two pages

items.title: Page 1, top: scope and structure.
items.text: Entities, sites and main suppliers in scope, who leads security, and whether it runs central, federated or hybrid.

items.title: Page 1, middle: the RACI.
items.text: One row per core process and one A per row. If a row needs two, split the process.

items.title: Page 1, bottom: the three lines.
items.text: Who operates, who monitors, who checks independently, and the date of the last independent review.

items.title: Page 2, top: services and decisions.
items.text: The service catalog, then the decision table: who accepts which risk, approves which exception and may stop which system.

items.title: Page 2, bottom: escalation and approval.
items.text: The phone chain with deputies, the next review date and management's approval. ENISA advises dating the organization chart and naming who updated it[^enisatig].

blocks.title: A RACI for six core processes
blocks.intro: A is the one person who answers for the outcome, R does the work, C is asked before and I is told after. Use your own job titles but keep one A per row.
items: **Patching.** A: head of IT. R: IT operations or the MSP. C: security, which sets deadlines from the patching sheet, and system owners for windows. I: management, about exploited flaws past deadline.
**Vulnerability management.** A: head of security. R: security scans, rates and tracks; system owners fix. C: IT operations. I: management, monthly. Record why a finding needs no fix[^ir2690].
**Access reviews.** A: each application's business owner. R: the owner's team leads, with lists from IT. C: security, for admin rights. I: internal audit. Document results and changes[^ir2690].

**Incident response.** A: head of security. R: the SOC or MDR and IT operations. C: legal, data protection, communications. I: management, insurer, authorities. Shutting down business is for the crisis team.

**Supplier onboarding.** A: the business owner who wants the supplier. R: procurement, with a contract manager per contract[^iiatp]. C: security, for tier and clauses. I: IT, to grant and later remove access.

**Exceptions.** A: the risk owner, at the level set in the risk register sheet. R: the requester, with the case, a compensating measure and an end date. C: security. I: management, via the open exceptions list.

blocks.title: Three lines, applied to security
items: **First line: whoever runs it.** IT operations, the MSP and application owners own the risk and run the controls[^iia3l], including patching and access reviews.
**Second line: security.** It sets standards, monitors and challenges the first line[^iia3l]. Where it also runs the firewall or EDR, have someone else check that part.
**Third line: someone independent.** Internal audit, or an external auditor. The IIA treats 12 months between running a process and assuring it as typically sufficient[^iia3l].

**Small companies may merge the first two.** ENISA lets IT staff take on security duties in small entities[^enisatig]. Never merge the third: where size rules out an independent reviewer, 2024/2690 requires other ways to keep reviews impartial[^ir2690].

blocks.title: Central, federated or hybrid
items: **Central.** One team sets the rules and runs security for everyone. Choose it when one IT team runs everything.
**Hybrid.** Central security owns the standards, risk register, MDR and scanning; units patch, review access and name champions. Choose it for most growing companies and for groups with plants.

**Federated.** Each unit has its own security officer, as the BSI suggests for large organizations[^std2002]. Choose it for legal entities with their own IT, since each one's management has its own BSIG duties[^bsig]. Keep one risk register across all of them.

blocks.title: What to buy and what to keep
items: **Buy what is rare or round the clock.** The NCSC suggests outsourcing functions that are seldom used or that you lack resources for, and notes that in-house teams know the business better[^ncscsoc]. Typical buys: 24/7 MDR (see the SOC and MDR sheet), pentests, an incident response retainer and a virtual CISO.
**Put a responsibility matrix in the MSP contract.** State what the MSP does and what stays with you, including who tracks end-of-life dates, as the NCSC advises[^ncscmsp].
**Know which line a provider is in.** The IIA places providers in the line of whoever engages them[^iia3l]. A pentest ordered by IT is first-line testing, not independent assurance.

**Keep decisions, risk acceptance and supplier oversight.** Outsourcing doesn't change accountability[^iia3l]. DORA has financial entities name a role to monitor ICT suppliers[^dora]; give every supplier an internal owner anyway.

blocks.title: Decision rights and escalation
items: **Let delegates accept smaller risks.** 2024/2690 allows acceptance by people with the authority to manage risks, if management gets adequate reports[^ir2690]. Set amounts and expiry with the risk register sheet.
**Pre-authorize containment.** The on-call engineer or MDR may isolate a device or disable an account without asking. Shutting down a business service is for the crisis team.

**Escalate on triggers.** The IIA expects quick escalation of any risk that reaches an unacceptable level[^iiacyber]. Use triggers such as an exploited flaw past deadline, an exception past expiry or a supplier refusing a key clause.
**Set when security must be asked.** Grundschutz++ requires defining when the security officer joins security-relevant projects[^std3001]; the security projects sheet covers the gates.

blocks.title: Security champions in business and IT teams
items: **Name one per team that holds risk.** IT operations, development, finance for payment changes, HR for joiners and leavers, and plant operations for OT.
**Put their time in writing.** OWASP advises formally allocating champions' time and getting management support, because formal priorities win when priorities conflict[^owaspsc].
**Give them tasks, not authority.** They triage findings, review risky changes and act as first contact in incidents. They don't approve exceptions or accept risk.

blocks.title: A service catalog of what security offers
items: **List each service with how to ask and how fast.** For example, project reviews in 5 working days, supplier checks in 10 and incident response at once.

**Cover the usual set.** Advice and project reviews, exceptions, vulnerability scanning, supplier checks, incident response, awareness and audit evidence, each with who delivers it: in-house, MDR or MSP.
**Say what security doesn't do.** It doesn't patch, grant access or sign supplier contracts. Name who does.

blocks.title: What the law and ISO 27001 say about roles
items: **NIS2 Article 20.** Management bodies approve the risk management measures, oversee their implementation, can be held liable and must take training[^nis2].
**BSIG § 38.** Management must implement the § 30 measures, oversee them and train regularly, and is liable to the entity for culpable damage[^bsig].

**Regulation 2024/2690.** Digital providers such as cloud and managed service providers assign roles and report them to management, have one person report directly to it, segregate conflicting duties and review roles regularly[^ir2690].
**DORA.** Financial entities other than microenterprises separate ICT risk management, control and internal audit, by the three lines of defense or an internal model[^dora].
**ISO/IEC 27001.** ENISA maps the roles duties of 2024/2690 to clause 5.3 and Annex A 5.2 to 5.4[^enisatig], so one RACI serves both.

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **The IIA replaced its Three Lines Model.** The Statement of Position of 8 July 2026[^iiasop] adds guidance for organizations without separate assurance functions and says outsourcing doesn't change accountability[^iia3l]. Recheck where you've merged lines.

**Internal audit must check cyber roles.** Since 5 February 2026, auditors giving cyber assurance must assess roles and quick escalation[^iiacyber]; since 15 September 2026, also who selects, manages and monitors suppliers[^iiatp]. Have your RACI ready.
**The BSI drew the line on delegation.** Its October 2026 curriculum lets management delegate the work but not responsibility and oversight, and lists a responsibility matrix as evidence[^bsicurr].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A RACI for every task.** Six processes and a decision table settle most disputes. Add a row only when a dispute comes back.
**An internal audit department in a small company.** Buy a yearly independent review instead, such as a certification audit or an auditor who neither runs nor advises on your IT.
**A target operating model deck.** Two pages people use beat 40 slides nobody opens. Write down how work is done today before you reorganize.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Two accountable people for one process.** Then nobody is. Split the process or pick one.
**Security as A for everything.** Then IT and the business stop treating patching and access as their job. Make the system's owner accountable.
**No deputies.** ENISA advises a deputy for each security role[^enisatig]. Name one for every A and test the phone chain twice a year.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: The managing director accepts risks and approves exceptions; the IT lead or MSP runs the controls.
Write the two pages with your MSP and approve them in a management meeting.
Get a yearly review from someone who neither runs nor advises on your IT.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Run hybrid, with champions in IT and business teams.
Keep the security role apart from the IT lead, as Grundschutz++ requires[^std3001]; the security team sheet covers where it reports.
Publish the service catalog and the decision table.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Name security officers per unit or entity under one group standard and one risk register.
Keep an assurance map of who checks which control, to find gaps and duplicated checks[^iia3l].
Under DORA, document the control function's independence from internal audit[^dora].

changes.text: First draft, based on the IIA's 2026 Three Lines Model and topical requirements, NIS2, BSIG § 38, Regulation 2024/2690 with ENISA's guidance, DORA and BSI guidance.
